u1:
My view is that moms should raise their own kids, inside a community where the care is really shared. The village can handle meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, and a lot of the fathering, but it should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. It's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing what she saw, but it's still a powerful picture. She talks about how the babies are carried with them and brought into adult life, how the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and how it doesn't fall on one tired parent to be their whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.

Experiments where kids don't sleep and live with their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and many loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.

I'd suggest taking a direct look at what's going on at Tamera's Children's Place instead of caricaturing it. To be honest, my own bias is still toward a system where kids interact with more people, without the parent-child bond being made ideologically inconvenient.
u2:
The Amish let their young people make the decision to join the church on their own when they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem far wilder and more universal than it is, but it's still a big deal that they're baptized as adults, because then belonging is a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If the kids never leave, the community has no way of knowing whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, see other ways of living, and disagree with the founders, without treating them as traitors for it.

Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.

The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. Kids who grow up without ever using money especially need a decent education in how the money world operates, and what to do when they have to deal with it: jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help.

They also need a good set of transferable skills and education, good relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community). It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, travel expenses, tools or a little money, but even if it can't, it can at least not make things worse by punishing people for leaving, or by holding back knowledge or records a young adult would need to function outside the community. No upbringing can provide perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.

It's possible that some of them will split off, either permanently, or into their own communities with different values, rather than wait decades to inherit the original one. And parents may experience that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
